dossiers.eurodollars.tldr.4: The name reportedly comes from the telex address of a Soviet bank in Paris, “Eurobank” [6]. The market then went through its crises: the collapse of Herstatt Bank in 1974 [7], the freezing of Iranian assets in 1979, including at US bank branches abroad [8], and the Libor scandal, involving the market's benchmark rate, which was discontinued on June 30, 2023 [9].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.6.title: The name: a telex address in Paris
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.6.paragrap: Where does the word “eurodollar” come from? According to the most widespread account, from a Soviet-owned bank based in Paris, the ==Banque commerciale pour l'Europe du Nord (BCEN)==. Its telegraphic address, the equivalent of an email address at the time, was ==“EUROBANK”== [6].

The dollars that communist countries deposited there, to keep them safe from US seizure, were called “Eurobank dollars,” then simply “eurodollars” [6]. The BCEN placed them with other European banks, which in turn lent them out again: the market was born [6].

Historians do not fully agree on the first episode: some cite communist China, which is said to have transferred its dollars to Paris as early as the Korean War, before the United States froze its assets; others point to Soviet transfers in the late 1950s to the Moscow Narodny Bank in London and to the BCEN [6]. ==An irony of history: the market that built the dollar's global power was launched by countries that distrusted the United States.==
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.7.title: June 26, 1974: the bankruptcy that gave its name to a risk
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.7.paragrap: The eurodollar market relies on constant exchanges between currencies: marks are sold for dollars, pounds for francs. These trades are not always settled at the same moment, because markets are not open at the same hours.

On ==June 26, 1974==, at 3:30 p.m. Frankfurt time, the German authorities shut down the small ==Herstatt Bank==, ruined by currency bets [7]. That day, some banks had already paid it marks in Frankfurt, while waiting for dollars due to arrive in New York a few hours later. They never arrived: its correspondent bank in New York blocked all its dollar payments [7].

The financial world discovered ==“Herstatt risk”== (or settlement risk): having paid your side of a trade without receiving the other side [7]. That same year, the central bankers of the major countries set up a committee in Basel to coordinate the supervision of international banks: the future ==Basel Committee==, which would write the main global rules on bank capital (“Basel I, II, III”) [7].

It was not until ==2002== and the creation of CLS, a bank that settles both sides of a trade at the same moment, that this risk was sharply reduced [7]. Even in 2025, part of foreign exchange trading remains exposed [7].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.7.plain.st: In the morning, a German bank pays marks to Herstatt in Frankfurt, in exchange for dollars promised for the afternoon in New York.
At 3:30 p.m., Frankfurt shuts Herstatt down [7]. New York has barely opened.
The promised dollars are never sent: the German bank has paid and received nothing [7].
Lesson learned: settle both sides of a trade at the same time, which CLS has done since 2002 [7].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.8.title: November 14, 1979: even in London, the dollar remains American
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.8.paragrap: On November 4, 1979, Iranian students took the staff of the US embassy in Tehran hostage. On November 14, Iran announced that it would withdraw its deposits from American banks [8]. That same day, President ==Jimmy Carter== signed an executive order ==freezing the Iranian state's assets== in the United States [8].

The surprise was the scope of the freeze: it also applied to dollar deposits held by ==branches of American banks abroad==, notably in London [8]. More than $5.6 billion in deposits and securities placed in these branches were blocked, out of a total frozen amount that would exceed $12 billion [8].

For the eurodollar market, it was a shock: people believed that dollars placed in London were beyond Washington's reach. ==The freeze showed that dollar money remains within reach of US law as soon as an American bank is in the loop.== It marked the beginning of the modern use of the dollar as a sanctions weapon (see the course on sanctions). The assets were only released with the Algiers Accords of January 1981, which freed the hostages.
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.9.title: Libor: the most important rate in the world… and the most rigged
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.9.paragrap: To lend eurodollars to each other, London banks needed a benchmark rate. This was ==Libor== (London Interbank Offered Rate): every day, a panel of large banks indicated the rate at which they thought they could borrow, and the average was taken. For decades, hundreds of trillions of dollars of credit, mortgages and financial products around the world were indexed to this rate.

In ==June 2012==, the scandal broke: the British bank ==Barclays== agreed to pay around ==£290 million== in fines to British and American authorities [9]. Investigations showed that, from August 2007 to early 2009, its executives had asked for artificially low rates to be submitted, so as to look healthier during the crisis [9]. Other banks were sanctioned afterwards, and traders were convicted.

The underlying problem: Libor was based on ==submissions==, not on actual transactions. The authorities decided to replace it with rates calculated from real trades: ==SOFR== in the United States, SONIA in the United Kingdom [9]. On ==June 30, 2023==, the last dollar Libor rates stopped being published: after more than fifty years, the eurodollar market's rate disappeared [9].
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.10.title: A timeline to remember
dossiers.eurodollars.sections.10.paragra: ==1950s==: communist countries place their dollars in Paris and London; the word “eurodollar” appears [1][6]. ==1969==: American banks take part via the Bahamas [1]. ==1973-1974==: petrodollars swell the market; Herstatt collapse and birth of the Basel Committee [7].

==1979==: the freezing of Iranian assets shows that London dollars remain within Washington's reach [8]. ==2007-2008==: dollar shortage, the Fed opens its swap lines [4]. ==2012==: Libor scandal [9]. ==2019==: about $13 trillion in dollar debt held by non-US banks [3]. ==2020==: swap lines revived with Covid [5]. ==2023==: end of Libor [9].
The common thread: ==a market born to escape the United States, which ended up strengthening the dollar's power and making the whole world dependent on the Fed in times of crisis.==

dossiers.ascenseur-social.hook: Earning more than your parents: it was almost guaranteed for an American born in 1940; it is a 50-50 chance for those born in the 1980s. Why? And what really helps a child move up: the city, the neighborhood, friends, school, university? A long course inspired by the work of Harvard economist Raj Chetty, with a detour through France.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.tldr.0: In the United States, about 90% of children born in 1940 ended up earning more than their parents; for those born in the 1980s, it is roughly 50% [1][2].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.tldr.1: Chances vary enormously from one city to another: a poor child has a 4.4% chance of reaching the richest fifth in Charlotte, 12.9% in San Jose [7].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.tldr.2: The neighborhood has a real effect: each year of childhood spent in a better environment brings the child about 4% closer to that neighborhood's outcomes [8]. And helping families search for housing raises the share of those who move to a high-opportunity neighborhood from 14% to 54% [9].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.tldr.3: Friends, university and exposure to occupations also matter: having friends from well-off backgrounds is one of the best predictors of upward mobility [5], and children from the top 1% are ten times more likely to become inventors than those from the poorer half [6].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.tldr.4: In France, it would take more than six generations for a low-income family to reach average income, according to the OECD [13]; a child of a senior executive is about 4.5 times more likely than a child of a manual worker to be among the richest 20% [14].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.0.par: Economists call ==absolute mobility== the share of children who, as adults, earn more than their parents did at the same age, once inflation is removed. It is a simple and telling way to measure the “American dream”: does each generation live better than the previous one?

In 2016, Raj Chetty's team (then at Stanford, now at Harvard, where he heads the Opportunity Insights lab) calculated it for every generation since 1940. To do so, it anonymously linked children's tax returns to those of their parents, covering tens of millions of households. The result: ==about 90% for children born in 1940, about 50% for those born in the 1980s== [1][2].

Why such a drop? Two explanations combine. Growth has slowed since the 1970s. And above all, its benefits have increasingly gone to the top of the ladder. The authors run a thought experiment: if recent growth had been shared like that of the 1940s and 1950s, ==more than 70% of the decline would be erased==; conversely, stronger but equally unequal growth would erase only a small part of it [1].

This diagnosis is debated: in 2022, economist Scott Winship found the same decline but, according to his calculations, faster growth would have raised mobility far more than a more equal distribution; he therefore disputes that it is mainly explained by rising inequality [3]. It is a good example of a debate among economists: ==everyone agrees on the number, not on its cause==.

This debate is not just theoretical. If the main cause is slowing growth, the priority is to revive it. If it is distribution, the priority is to share its benefits better: wages, taxes, education. Depending on the answer, different policies are proposed.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.0.pla: A factory worker born in 1940 grows up in a fast-growing America, where everyone's wages are rising.
As an adult, he earns much more than his father: this is the case for 9 out of 10 children of his generation [1].
His grandson, born in 1984, enters the job market when growth mostly benefits the highest earners.
He now has only a 50-50 chance of earning more than his parents [1][2].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.1.tit: Two ways to measure: moving up, or changing places
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.1.par: Absolute mobility has a flaw: it depends heavily on overall growth. If the whole economy gets richer, almost everyone earns more than their parents, even if nobody changes rank. Economists therefore also look at ==relative mobility==: does a child born at the bottom of the ladder end up higher than their parents in their generation's income ranking?

To measure it, families are sorted into five groups of equal size, the ==quintiles==: the poorest 20%, then the next 20%, and so on up to the richest 20%. The question becomes: ==what is the probability that a child born in the bottom quintile reaches the top quintile?== If there were no link between background and success, it would be 20%.

The two measures tell different stories. A country can have high absolute mobility (everyone gets richer) and low relative mobility (everyone stays in their place), or the reverse. ==The “American dream” mixes the two==: living better than your parents, and having a chance to move up whatever your starting point.

These figures only measure income. They say nothing about health, happiness or the job people do. But income has a big advantage: it is recorded for almost everyone in tax data, which makes it possible to follow millions of children, not just a few thousand surveyed.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.1.exa: “7.5% of children from the bottom quintile reach the top quintile” means: out of 1,000 children born among the poorest 20%, 75 end up as adults among the richest 20%. In a world where background did not matter at all, there would be 200. The closer the figure gets to 20%, the more “mobile” the society.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.2.tit: A map of opportunity: Charlotte versus San Jose
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.2.par: In 2014, Chetty and his colleagues Nathaniel Hendren, Patrick Kline and Emmanuel Saez published a map of mobility in the United States, area by area, based on tax data for more than 40 million children [7]. The surprise was the size of the gaps within a single country.

A child born in the poorest 20% has ==a 4.4% chance of reaching the richest 20% if they grow up in Charlotte, North Carolina, compared with 12.9% in San Jose, California== [7]: almost three times as much. Same country, same currency, same federal laws, and yet very different chances.

The researchers looked at what high-mobility areas have in common. Five features stand out: ==less segregation between rich and poor neighborhoods, less income inequality, better primary schools, more social ties (associations, community life) and more stable families== [7].

The authors warn: these are ==correlations, not proven causes== [7]. A city may have good schools and high mobility because it attracts families who invest heavily in their children. To find out whether the place itself has an effect, another method is needed: following children who move.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.3.tit: Tell me where you grow up…
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.3.par: To find out whether the neighborhood really has an effect, researchers revisited a real-life experiment from the 1990s: ==Moving to Opportunity==. Families living in very poor public housing were selected by lottery: some received a voucher to rent in a less poor neighborhood, others did not.

Because chance decides, the two groups can be compared as in a drug trial. For a long time, the results were disappointing: adults' incomes had barely changed. But in 2015, Chetty's team looked at the children once they had grown up: ==those who moved before age 13 earn about 31% more== than those who stayed in their original neighborhood [4]. For those who moved as teenagers, the gain disappears.

A second study, of millions of families who move for all sorts of reasons, clarifies the mechanism. When a family moves to an area where children do better, ==its children's outcomes move closer to those of local children by about 4% per year of childhood spent there== [8]. And in the other direction, moving to a less favorable area costs about 4% per year [8].

To separate the effect of the place from that of the family, researchers compare siblings: when a family moves, the younger child spends more years in the new neighborhood than the older one. If the younger child does better, within the same family, it is the place that has the effect [8]. Conclusion: ==it is not only the address that matters, it is the time spent in a good environment during childhood==.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.3.pla: 1990s: families living in very poor public housing sign up for a federal program.
A lottery decides who receives a voucher to rent in a less poor neighborhood.
Researchers follow the children for twenty years using tax data.
Those who moved before age 13 earn about 31% more as adults [4]; the earlier the move, the bigger the gain, about 4% per year of childhood spent in the better neighborhood [8].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.4.tit: Helping families move: the Seattle experiment
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.4.par: If the neighborhood matters so much, why don't low-income families move to high-opportunity neighborhoods on their own? In the United States, many already receive housing assistance (the “Housing Choice Voucher”) that can be used almost anywhere. Yet most stay in poor neighborhoods.

In 2018, Chetty and researchers from MIT and Harvard launched a randomized trial with the housing authorities of Seattle and King County: ==Creating Moves to Opportunity==. Families in the test group received, on top of their usual assistance, information about high-opportunity neighborhoods, support in preparing their rental application, help with their search, modest financial support (security deposit, fees), and advisers who reached out to landlords [9].

Results from the first year: ==54% of supported families moved to a high-opportunity neighborhood, compared with about 14% in the group without support== [9]. Families were not required to choose these neighborhoods and kept their assistance whatever they decided [9].

Chetty's lesson: segregation in Seattle does not mainly come from families' deep preferences for certain neighborhoods, but from concrete obstacles: lack of information, reluctant landlords, upfront costs, complicated paperwork [9]. ==A small, well-placed nudge changes a lot.==
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.4.pla: why housing assistance is not enough
A single mother receives a housing voucher: she can rent almost anywhere.
But she does not know which neighborhoods have good schools, landlords in the nicer neighborhoods do not call her back, and she cannot afford the security deposit.
An adviser shows her the high-opportunity neighborhoods, helps her prepare her application, calls landlords and advances the deposit [9].
With this support, more than one family in two moves to a high-opportunity neighborhood, compared with one in seven without it [9].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.5.tit: Tell me who your friends are…
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.5.par: In 2022, Chetty's team published a massive study in the journal Nature, conducted with Meta: the friendships of ==72 million American Facebook users== aged 25 to 44, or 21 billion friendship links, matched to their city, high school and university [5].

It measures ==“economic connectedness”==: the share of friends from well-off backgrounds among people from low-income backgrounds. In some cities, low-income people have almost as many well-off friends as the average; in others, almost none. And this measure predicts a place's upward mobility better than most other factors studied, far better than the density of friendships or civic engagement [5].

Why do friends matter so much? They provide information (about studies, scholarships, jobs that are hiring), role models (“if he did it, I can do it”), norms (going to university becomes normal) and sometimes contacts for an internship or a job.

The study also shows where the lack of cross-class friendships comes from. Half comes from ==exposure==: the groups do not cross paths, because they live in different neighborhoods and go to different schools. The other half comes from what researchers call ==“friending bias”==: even when they meet in the same high school, they rarely form bonds, for example because the school separates them into different tracks or activities [5].

Practical consequence: to foster these ties, it is not enough to mix students in the same building. There also need to be places where they do things together: mixed classes, clubs, sports, joint projects.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.6.par: In 2018, Chetty's team studied mobility by race and ethnicity, using data on 20 million children and their parents followed from 1989 to 2015 [10]. Black and American Indian Americans have much lower upward mobility and much higher downward mobility than white Americans [10].

The most striking finding concerns boys. ==With identical parental income, Black boys earn less as adults than white boys in 99% of American neighborhoods== [10]. And the gap persists even between boys who grew up in the same neighborhood [10].

The researchers rule out several explanations. Differences in ability do not account for these gaps, and neighborhood resources, such as school quality, are not enough on their own to explain them [10].

Their conclusion: reducing the gap will require efforts that cross neighborhood and social class boundaries, and that specifically target the mobility of Black men [10]. This work shows the power of data, but also its limits: it says where and how much better than why.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.7.tit: University: a ladder for everyone, or for a few?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.7.par: University is often presented as the great social ladder. In 2017, Chetty's team published the ==“mobility report cards” of American colleges==, based on tax data on more than 30 million students enrolled between 1999 and 2013 [12].

For each institution, they calculate a ==mobility rate==: the share of students from the poorest 20% (access), multiplied by the share of these students who reach the richest 20% as adults (success). On average, this rate is 1.7% [12].

The champions are not the most prestigious. The big private universities have a very high success rate, but admit very few poor students. It is ==mid-tier public universities, such as those of the City University of New York (CUNY) or California State (Cal State), that move the most children from the bottom to the top== [12]. The authors point out that these are observations, not proof that the university is the cause [12].

In 2023, another study looked at admissions to the most selective universities, the “Ivy-Plus” (Ivy League, Stanford, MIT, Duke, Chicago). ==With equal entrance test scores, children from the top 1% are more than twice as likely to attend as those from the middle class== [11]. Nearly half of this advantage comes from the preference for children of alumni, “legacies”; another part from recruited athletes and more favorable “non-academic” ratings [11].

Why does it matter? Because these universities train a large share of leaders: the study shows that being admitted significantly increases the chances of reaching the top 1% of earners and of going to a major research university or a prestigious company [11]. ==Who gets into these schools partly decides who will run the country.==
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.7.exa: A university admits 20% of its students from the poorest families (access), and 30% of them reach the richest 20% as adults (success). Its mobility rate is 20% × 30% = 6%: out of 100 students, 6 made the whole journey from the bottom to the top. A prestigious university with 4% poor students and 60% success has only 4% × 60% = 2.4%.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.8.par: Another famous study by the team, published in 2019: who becomes an inventor in the United States? The researchers cross-referenced patent filings with parental income and school test scores [6].

The finding is stark: ==children from the top 1% of incomes are ten times more likely to become inventors than those from the poorer half== [6]. Is it because they are more gifted? Math scores in elementary school do predict well who invents. But even among the best math students, rich children invent much more than low-income children [6].

The key is ==exposure==: growing up in a city with many inventors, or having inventor parents, sharply increases the chances of becoming one, and often in the same specific field as the adults you were around [6]. According to the authors, only a small part of the gaps (about 6%) is explained by differences in ability at birth [6].

The authors draw a powerful idea from this: ==much talent is lost simply because it has never seen the job up close==. These are the “lost Einsteins.” Mentoring, internships and meetings with researchers in schools in low-income neighborhoods could recover some of them [6].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.9.par: Chetty's data cover the United States, but the question arises everywhere. In 2018, the OECD published a report with a telling title: ==“A Broken Social Elevator?”== [13]. On average in rich countries, it would take about five generations, or 150 years, for a child from a poor family to reach average income; two to three in the Nordic countries, nine or more in some emerging countries [13].

For France, the estimate is ==more than six generations== [13], more than the rich-country average. A paradox often pointed out: France redistributes a lot through taxes and benefits, which reduces gaps in living standards, but social background weighs heavily on qualifications and on income before redistribution.

That same year, the public agency France Stratégie published ==“Born under the same star?”==, a study on the link between parents' occupations and the living standards of their children as adults [14]. A child of a senior executive is about ==4.5 times more likely than a child of a manual worker to belong to the richest 20%== [14]. A son of a doctor or lawyer has about a 50-50 chance of being there, a son of a teacher 40%, but only 12% of children of care workers or domestic workers [14].

France Stratégie's diagnosis: ==“inequality of opportunity in France is first and foremost inequality of educational opportunity”== [14]. Children of executives go on to long studies much more often, and qualifications then weigh heavily on income. Neighborhood, networks and exposure to occupations, highlighted by Chetty, add to this educational inequality.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.9.pla: Inès, the daughter of an executive, has parents who know about the preparatory classes, the grandes écoles and their entrance exams.
Karim, the son of a factory worker, has equally good grades, but nobody around him has done long studies.
Inès aims for a grande école; Karim chooses a short program, for lack of information and role models.

As adults, the gap in qualifications becomes a gap in income: this is the mechanism France Stratégie describes [14]. A mentor or an internship could have changed things for Karim, as research on exposure suggests [6].
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.10.pa: ==Measuring in order to act.== By mapping the chances in each neighborhood (their “Opportunity Atlas” is public), this research helps target housing assistance, schools and mentoring programs where they make the biggest difference. The Seattle experiment is a direct example [9].

==Investing early.== Since the neighborhood effect builds up year after year during childhood [8], acting early pays off more. An Opportunity Insights study of 133 US public policies shows that investments in the health and education of low-income children often have the best return, and that many ==paid for themselves== through the taxes later paid by these children once they became adults [15].

==Changing the question.== Instead of asking only “how much should be redistributed?”, we also ask “where and how can every child be given a chance?”: neighborhood, school, networks, role models, access to university.

==Using data.== These studies were only possible by anonymously linking large-scale tax data. This is the method Chetty teaches at Harvard: using big databases to answer concrete social questions, and testing solutions through randomized trials.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.sections.11.pa: ==One measure among others.== Absolute mobility depends heavily on overall growth; relative mobility tells another story. And income is not everything: health, satisfaction or chosen occupation do not appear in these figures.

==Correlation or cause?== The map of opportunity [7] and cross-class friendships [5] are linked to upward mobility, but it is not necessarily the place or the friendship that causes it. That is why randomized experiments, such as Moving to Opportunity and Seattle, matter so much [4][9].
==Debated causes.== The role of inequality in the decline of mobility is debated among economists [1][3].

==American data.== The mechanisms (where you live, friends, role models) probably apply elsewhere, but their effects must be measured country by country. In France, data linking parents and children are scarcer, which makes detailed comparisons more difficult.

==Solutions at scale?== An experiment that works with a few hundred families does not necessarily work for a whole country: if all low-income families moved to the same high-opportunity neighborhoods, those neighborhoods would themselves change.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.forMe: Your path does not depend only on your grades: your neighborhood, your school, the people around you and the jobs you have been able to see up close also matter. For a student, it is one more reason to seek out new encounters, internships and mentors, and, when you can, to open the door in turn for younger people who do not have these contacts.

dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.0.q: What share of Americans born in the 1980s earn more than their parents?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.0.explain: It was about 90% for children born in 1940; it fell to about 50% for those born in the 1980s.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.1.q: What is the difference between absolute mobility and relative mobility?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.1.options: Absolute: earning more than your parents; relative: changing rank on the income ladder
Absolute: in euros; relative: in dollars
Absolute: for the rich; relative: for the poor
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.1.explain: If everyone gets richer, absolute mobility is high even if nobody changes rank.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.2.q: In a world where background did not matter, what share of children from the bottom quintile would reach the top quintile?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.2.explain: Each quintile contains 20% of the population: with no link between background and success, everyone would have a 20% chance of reaching the top.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.3.q: Does a poor child have the same chances of moving up in Charlotte and in San Jose?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.3.options: Yes, it is the same country
No: 4.4% in Charlotte versus 12.9% in San Jose
No: the chances are better in Charlotte
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.3.explain: Nearly three times better chances in San Jose, according to the map by Chetty, Hendren, Kline and Saez (2014).
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.4.q: What did the Moving to Opportunity experiment show?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.4.options: Children who move young to a less poor neighborhood earn more as adults
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.4.explain: Children who moved before age 13 earn about 31% more as adults; for teenagers, the gain disappears.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.5.q: In the Seattle experiment, what raised the share of families moving to a high-opportunity neighborhood from 14% to 54%?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.5.options: Support: information, help with the application, contacts with landlords, financial assistance
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.5.explain: Families remained free to choose: it was concrete obstacles that held them back, not their preferences.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.6.options: The share of friends from well-off backgrounds among people from low-income backgrounds
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.6.explain: It is one of the best predictors of upward mobility, according to the 2022 study of 72 million Facebook users.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.7.q: Which American universities move the most children from the bottom to the top?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.7.options: Mid-tier public universities, such as CUNY or Cal State
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.7.explain: The most prestigious have high success rates but admit very few poor students; CUNY and Cal State combine access and success.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.8.options: Gifted children who do not become inventors for lack of exposure to innovation
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.8.explain: Children from the top 1% are ten times more likely to invent; seeing inventors up close is key.
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.9.q: According to France Stratégie, where does inequality of opportunity in France mainly come from?
dossiers.ascenseur-social.quiz.9.explain: Children of executives more often go on to long studies, and qualifications then weigh on income.
